newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew in darkness, hit by new power problems.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew in darkness, hit by new power problems.

text.p: The Russian-American crew of the Mir space station shut down all unnecessary systems on Thursday, plunging the crippled ship into darkness as engineers scrambled to sort out a new navigational problem.
Officials insisted the three-man crew, whose Russian commander has reported a minor heart problem, were in no immediate danger.
But the rise in tension was palpable at Mission Control outside Moscow in the latest drama since a collision on June 25, which cut power by up to half and nearly cost the cosmonauts their lives.
"Close down all unnecessary systems," the duty mission controller ordered them on Thursday.
"Shut it down! Shut it down!" he barked into a microphone to Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev as specialists crowded round.

Officials told Reuters there was no light aboard and the power supply was at the bare minimum needed just to keep Mir going following an unexplained malfunction in the system that keeps its solar batteries lined up with the Sun.
Spokesman Valery Lyndin told Reuters: "There was a drop in the power supply...It has fallen to the minimum level needed to run the ship." But he added: "There is no threat to the crew."
Kathleen Maliga, a NASA official at Mission Control in the suburb of Korolyov, told Reuters: "They're safe and they're taking steps to restore power. Most systems are off."
"This has happened before," she added. "It's a similar situation to what happened after the accident."
One Russian official said: "We've already had similar cases. It's not serious but it is unpleasant." Another added: "I think it'll last a day or two."

The crew, including British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale, 40, are due next week to try to repair cables cut in the original accident, when quick thinking saved the cosmonauts' lives by sealing off the module punctured in the collision.
The crew have been living in relative darkness and inactivity for three weeks since then.

Adding to the problems, commander Tsibliyev, 43, suffered a slight heart flutter this week, probably due to stress, and Foale was asked to take his place alongside flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39, during the two-man repair job.

NASA and Russian officials are still studying whether Foale, an astrophysicist, has had adequate training in working in spacesuits for the task of reconnecting the severed cables to three important solar batteries. If not, it would be put off for a Russian-French relief crew, which arrives on August 7.

Since the accident, the worst in its 11 years in space, Mir has been dogged by repeated failures in the gyroscopic system that keeps its remaining solar panels lined up on the Sun as the craft hurtles round the Earth in orbit.
That creates a vicious circle, depriving the station of more power and making it even harder to realign it. The problem is countered by firing rocket motors, but that uses up fuel.
Russian officials, whose agency partly depends on the foreign cash Mir brings in to keep the post-Soviet space industry afloat, insist they will not abandon the station.
Mir is a test bed for the future international space station Alpha, due to start being assembled in orbit next year.

However, if conditions became untenable, the Mir crew could take to their Soyuz escape capsule and return home, probably condemning Mir to a premature end and posing a headache on Earth where the 140-tonne complex would come down with a crash.
